Consider the ranking model under active development. When a developer commits code changes, the CI pipeline pulls the specified dataset version, performs feature preprocessing, and initiates model training. Experiments are tracked in a registry such as MLflow [@mlflow_website], which logs loss curves and registers model artifacts. After passing automated offline validation, the model is containerized and deployed to a staging cluster. If the candidate satisfies staging validation, the pipeline executes a canary rollout (@sec-ml-operations-model-deployment-b9b9), gradually shifting production query traffic to the new model while monitoring inference latency and error rates. If a performance regression emerges, traffic automatically rolls back to the previous model checkpoint.

CI/CD becomes foundational when systems release models repeatedly or carry meaningful production risk, turning ad hoc experimentation into structured, repeatable deployment. Scaling beyond one pipeline requires reusable components and explicitly specified artifact schemas.

::: {#exmp-ml-ops-google-tfx-production-ml-pipelines .callout-example title="Google TFX production ML pipelines"}

**Scenario**: Google's production experience motivated TensorFlow Extended (TFX), a set of reusable components for production ML pipelines [@baylor2017]. As pipelines multiply, ad hoc handoffs make validation, lineage, and reproducibility difficult.

**Diagnosis**: Each stage needs explicit validation and metadata so a deployed model can be traced to the data, transformations, code, and evaluation that produced it.

**Systems lesson**: Directed acyclic graph orchestration alone does not establish reproducibility. Standardized components and ML Metadata (MLMD), a store that records the inputs and outputs of every pipeline component run, preserve lineage through recorded inputs and transformations.

:::

#### Training pipelines {#sec-ml-operations-training-pipelines-2dcf}

CI/CD pipelines orchestrate the overall workflow, but training itself requires specialized compute infrastructure. Model training\index{Training pipeline!automated ML workflows} builds on the single-node parallel execution primitives that training systems already provide. Within MLOps, training activities become components of a reproducible pipeline supporting continual experimentation and production deployment.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The single-node data- and model-parallel execution that training pipelines schedule is established in @sec-model-training-singlenode-multigpu-training-c87f.
:::

Frameworks such as TensorFlow [@abadi2016tensorflow], PyTorch [@paszke2019pytorch], and Keras [@keras] supply modular components for model architectures and optimization routines. Operational discipline determines which exploratory training routines graduate into versioned, tested retraining jobs, and under what execution triggers.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The criteria for selecting a framework are established in @sec-ml-frameworks-model-requirements-2e01.
:::

Training scripts and environment configurations are version-controlled with Git [@git] and hosted on GitHub [@github]. Interactive Jupyter [@jupyter] notebooks accelerate prototyping by coupling code, inline visualizations, and execution state, but running them unaltered in production pipelines introduces severe operational liabilities.

##### Notebooks in production {#sec-ml-operations-notebooks-production-7016}

Automated CI/CD pipelines assume deterministic and reproducible code execution, but Jupyter notebooks\index{Jupyter Notebook!production risk} violate this assumption through persistent kernel state. In an interactive session, cells can be executed out of linear order, creating hidden memory dependencies that cannot be reproduced from a clean interpreter restart. A common production failure occurs when development relies on cells executed in sequence 1-3-2; a scheduled batch runner executing top-to-bottom (1-2-3) fails due to undefined variables or altered intermediate tensors.

Testing difficulties compound this state vulnerability. Standard unit-testing harnesses and mocking frameworks do not interface cleanly with interactive notebook documents. Cell-level assertions are rarely parameterized or wired into test runners, leaving notebooks significantly less tested than modular Python code.

Two tools help. Papermill\index{Papermill!notebook parameterization} enables parameterization and headless execution of notebooks, injecting runtime configurations and executing cells top-to-bottom as discrete pipeline stages [@papermillDocs]. nbconvert converts validated notebooks into static executable Python scripts for production environments [@nbconvertDocs], exposing exported code to linters and CI test runners. Teams must still select or refactor exploratory cells and verify clean, ordered execution.

Extracting code from notebooks into tested modules introduces refactoring overhead, but it prevents hidden state assumptions from causing training-serving skew in production, a silent failure whose cost grows with every day it goes undetected, as the silent-failure calculation in the monitoring discussion shows (notebook \ref{nbk-ml-ops-cost-silent-failures}).

Modular training logic also allows a pipeline to schedule repeatable experiments within the node's resource budget. Concurrent runs compete for accelerator memory, host preprocessing capacity, and storage bandwidth; enforcing resource limits recorded alongside each run's configuration keeps experiments within the capacity reserved for them. If execution can be interrupted, checkpoint-and-resume (@sec-model-training-training-state-checkpoints-5b3e) preserves completed training work without requiring the entire run to restart.

How often to run this pipeline depends on evidence that only production monitoring supplies, so @sec-ml-operations-retraining-decisions-7d3a takes up the decision after monitoring. A pipeline that can run on demand still produces only candidates, and validation decides which of them may ship.

#### Model validation {#sec-ml-operations-model-validation-a891}

Training pipelines produce model candidates; model validation\index{Model validation!candidate selection}\index{Model validation!predeployment assessment} determines which candidates merit production deployment. Unlike research evaluation, where a model that beats a benchmark on a static test set may be considered successful, production validation must assess operational readiness under representative conditions and establish the monitoring and rollback controls needed after the distribution changes. This is where MLOps manages the verification gap\index{Verification gap!MLOps management} (principle \ref{pri-verification-gap}) rather than closing it. No test suite covers the deployment population, so validation keeps re-estimating performance as that population changes.

The evaluation process begins with performance testing against a holdout test set\index{Holdout test set!performance evaluation} sampled to represent the current production population and refreshed as that population changes. Core metrics such as accuracy, AUC, precision, recall, and F1 score [@rainio2024] are computed and tracked longitudinally to detect degradation from data drift [@ibm_data_drift], the shift of the input distribution away from the one the model trained on. @Sec-ml-operations-model-infrastructure-monitoring-3988 shows how such drift appears in live telemetry.

Beyond static evaluation, production pipelines expose candidate weights to live traffic in controlled stages\index{Deployment!controlled, risk mitigation} (shadow, canary, and blue-green deployment) while bounding the blast radius, and @sec-ml-operations-model-deployment-b9b9 develops each. Validation defines the evidence every stage must produce before a candidate advances.

Evaluating candidates under identical operational conditions is the prerequisite for a sound promotion decision; a candidate that shows apparent metric gains simply because it was evaluated against a differing traffic slice or temporal window confounds model quality with data variance. Cloud ML platforms support controlled evaluation through request replay, shadow serving, and synthetic load testing. The comparison must also be recorded: experiment trackers such as Weights & Biases [@weights_biases_platform] log the data slice, time window, configuration, and metrics used for each candidate, so a promotion decision can be audited and repeated under the same conditions.

While automated validation gates protect against regressions on primary aggregate metrics, production validation also requires auditing slices and long-tail behavior. Automated test suites often mask severe performance drops on underrepresented subpopulations or safety-critical edge cases. Production architectures combine automated gating with policy reviews, particularly for models deployed in regulated domains. This multi-stage validation discipline bridges offline evaluation with live production monitoring, ensuring that candidate models satisfy accuracy, latency, and safety invariants before receiving unconstrained serving traffic.

### Infrastructure integration {#sec-ml-operations-infrastructure-integration-summary-cb2f}

Development infrastructure addresses two of the three critical system interfaces. Feature stores and data versioning reduce inconsistency at the data-model interface by centralizing and tracking feature access across training and serving. CI/CD pipelines, model registries, and validation gates stabilize the model-infrastructure interface by automating the transition from trained weights to containerized services with rollback capability.

These controls prepare an artifact for release. The third interface, production monitoring, closes the operational loop by tracking whether predictive quality holds as inputs and operating conditions change, but the release must come first.

## Releasing Models {#sec-ml-operations-production-operations-b76d}

A model that passes every offline gate has still not made a single production decision. Between the validated checkpoint and the first user-facing prediction lie packaging, conversion to a serving runtime, staged exposure to live traffic, and a path back if the new version misbehaves, and at each step the artifact users see can drift from the artifact that was evaluated. Deployment transforms a static checkpoint into a versioned, reproducible execution artifact. Serving then allocates accelerator memory, stages input batches, and schedules compute kernels to satisfy latency SLOs under dynamic request loads. Operations owns the seams between the two: proving that what ships is what was validated, limiting how much traffic a bad version can reach, and keeping rollback fast enough to use. On the ranking service each of those seams also costs memory, because any control that keeps two versions alive must hold two copies of the embedding tables.

### Infrastructure as code {#sec-ml-operations-infrastructure-management-bf8f}

Three failures show how an unmanaged environment drifts away from the one that was validated. A model works in staging but fails in production because someone manually provisioned a different GPU type. A training job crashes because a colleague's experiment consumed all available memory. An inference service cannot scale because its resource quotas were set through an informal message six months earlier. These failures share a root cause: infrastructure managed through manual processes rather than code.

**Infrastructure as code (IaC)**\index{Infrastructure as code!ML systems} treats infrastructure configuration as software (version-controlled, reviewed, tested, and automatically executed) rather than something configured through graphical interfaces or command-line tools. Changes are tracked, configurations can be tested before deployment, and environments can be reliably reproduced.

The specific tool matters less than the property it enforces. Infrastructure-as-code tools such as Terraform\index{Terraform!infrastructure as code} [@terraform] version infrastructure definitions alongside application code, so a team can reproduce the accelerator type, network policy, storage permissions, and scaling limits of a training or serving environment on any cloud provider or on-premises hardware, and can audit and test those definitions in the same CI/CD pipelines as the model. Containerization\index{Containerization!ML deployment} provides the same reproducibility boundary for runtime dependencies. Docker [@docker] packages the model, libraries, and serving code into an isolated unit, and orchestration systems such as Kubernetes\index{Kubernetes!ML orchestration} [@kubernetes_orchestration] deploy that unit repeatedly while keeping resource allocation, scaling, and health management explicit.

To absorb spikes during hyperparameter tuning and surges in prediction traffic, teams use autoscaling\index{Autoscaling!ML workloads}[^fn-autoscaling-ml-workloads] [@aws_autoscaling], which adjusts compute capacity from usage metrics to balance performance and cost. The same infrastructure definitions must also cover on-premises and edge targets when latency, privacy, or regulation keeps part of a deployment off the cloud.

[^fn-autoscaling-ml-workloads]: **ML autoscaling**\index{Autoscaling!ML cold-start trade-off}: Autoscaling adjusts capacity based on demand signals [@aws_autoscaling], but ML serving adds constraints absent from stateless web services. Autoscaling decisions must account for model loading time (cold-start overhead), GPU memory fragmentation, and batching behavior in addition to CPU utilization. Scaling up too slowly violates latency SLOs; scaling down too aggressively forces repeated cold starts that degrade p99 latency.

Infrastructure as code addresses how to provision resources reproducibly, but operators must still decide when and how much capacity to allocate. ML workloads break the assumptions of conventional web provisioning. Training jobs demand high-concurrency bursts across distributed accelerator topologies, creating friction between cluster utilization efficiency and time-to-solution. Inference services require sustained baseline allocations with rapid elastic scale-out to absorb request spikes under strict tail-latency SLOs. The utilization targets in @sec-ml-operations-hardware-utilization-patterns-5c10 turn these competing demands into measurable provisioning goals.

### Validating the serving artifact {#sec-ml-operations-model-format-optimization-c9d6}

The artifact that reaches the serving fleet is rarely the checkpoint that passed evaluation. Before deployment, the model is usually compiled from eager framework code into a static graph for a specific runtime and often lowered in precision. Each conversion trades portability for speed, and each can change what the model computes, so the operational obligation is to prove that the converted artifact still behaves like the model that was validated.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Inference runtimes and the precision choices they support for serving are established in @sec-model-serving-inference-runtime-selection-5eef.
:::

That proof must target the failure modes that conversion introduces silently\index{Model Optimization!conversion validation}. Consider a team that deploys an INT8-quantized model after verifying only throughput improvement: classification accuracy drops on rare but high-value edge cases, and the degradation goes undetected for weeks because aggregate metrics remain within SLO bounds. The first validation layer is numerical equivalence, comparing optimized outputs against the original model on a representative test set with application-specific divergence thresholds. That check is necessary but insufficient, because a static calibration slice is not live traffic: rare inputs, out-of-distribution examples, and subgroup-specific cases can expose quantization artifacts that aggregate test metrics hide, so the comparison must be disaggregated by the same cohorts that production monitoring tracks (@sec-ml-operations-production-monitoring-5e1b).

The second layer is operational validation. Memory footprint must be measured at peak runtime utilization, including dynamic allocations during inference, since some optimizations trade increased runtime memory for computational speed. Warm-up behavior varies by runtime: Accelerated Linear Algebra (XLA)\index{XLA!warm-up compilation} may JIT-compile kernels during initial execution, whereas TensorRT\index{TensorRT!model optimization} selects tactics and builds an engine before deployment; loading that engine can still add startup latency. Runtime version compatibility then closes the loop. Deployment configurations need explicit version pinning\index{Version pinning!inference runtime}, because even a minor runtime upgrade can change kernel selection, and with it both latency and numerical results, in an artifact whose weights never changed. An unpinned runtime is an untracked input to @eq-model-reproducibility.

### Model deployment {#sec-ml-operations-model-deployment-b9b9}

Consider a new version of the ranking model that beats its predecessor offline. An engineer exports the weights, copies them to a production server, and discovers that the model scores nearly every item the same, because the production server runs a different version of the feature extraction library and produces inputs the model has never seen. This scenario illustrates why deployment is a systems engineering problem rather than a simple file transfer. Packaging, testing, and tracking ML models\index{Model deployment!packaging and serving} for reliable production deployment requires treating the model weights, runtime dependencies, and preprocessing configuration as a single deployable unit. Containerizing the model artifact and serving runtime[^fn-containerization-ml-deploy] packages user-space dependencies, runtime libraries, and environment variables into an immutable image, enforcing environment parity between development and cluster nodes.

[^fn-containerization-ml-deploy]: **Containerization for ML deployment**\index{Containerization!environment parity}: Docker [@docker] packages code with dependencies into portable units; Kubernetes [@burns2016] orchestrates those units across clusters. Containerization addresses the $\text{Environment}_\ArtifactVersion$ term in @eq-model-reproducibility partially by capturing user-space dependencies as a versioned artifact; host kernels, drivers, and hardware remain external dependencies.

Production deployment requires frameworks that handle model packaging, versioning, and integration with serving infrastructure. Tools like MLflow and model registries manage these deployment artifacts [@chen2020], while serving-specific frameworks handle the runtime optimization and scaling requirements. Before full-scale rollout, teams deploy updated models to staging or QA environments[^fn-staging-validation-ops] to rigorously test performance.

[^fn-staging-validation-ops]: **Staging validation**\index{Staging validation!probabilistic adequacy}: ML staging adds probabilistic adequacy checks to conventional functional and operational validation. A model can pass unit tests and still fail in production because the test data does not reflect the deployment distribution, so rollout gates must compare prediction statistics, evaluation slices, and business guardrails against calibrated thresholds rather than rely on unit tests alone.

Three release strategies carry that staging validation into live traffic. **Shadow deployments**\index{Shadow deployment!production validation}[^fn-shadow-deploy-ml] duplicate live production traffic asynchronously to a candidate model without returning its inferences to users, enabling latency and output comparison without direct user exposure; accuracy still requires labels or another ground-truth reference. **Canary deployments**\index{Canary deployment!risk-controlled rollout}[^fn-canary-deploy-ml] route a small share of user traffic to the candidate and keep ramping that share toward full traffic as long as no regression appears under live load. **Blue-green deployments**\index{Blue-green deployment!zero-downtime updates}[^fn-bluegreen-deploy-ml] maintain parallel environments for router-level cutover and rapid rollback. Each strategy reduces a different release risk, but none removes the need for tested rollback procedures and production monitoring.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The shadow-then-canary staged rollout, and the evidence each stage contributes before full release, are established in @sec-ml-workflow-offline-online-evaluation-3a6b.
:::

[^fn-shadow-deploy-ml]: **Shadow deployment**\index{Shadow deployment!inference cost}: Economically justified when its expected reduction in rollout loss exceeds the cost of shadow infrastructure for duplicated inference without serving results.

[^fn-canary-deploy-ml]: **Canary deployment**\index{Canary deployment!statistical validation}: The ML-specific challenge is that a "failure" is statistical degradation, not a deterministic crash: detecting a small accuracy difference with high confidence can require thousands of inferences, creating a tension between decision speed and statistical power that determines minimum canary duration.

[^fn-bluegreen-deploy-ml]: **Blue-green deployment**\index{Blue-green deployment!duplicate capacity}: Maintains two comparable production environments, "blue" (serving current traffic) and "green" (running the candidate), then switches traffic in a routing change once the green environment passes validation. Because rollback is a traffic flip rather than a staged drain, recovery can be faster than a gradual canary for stateless services. The trade-off is extra infrastructure during the switch, so blue-green wins over canary when brief duplicate capacity is acceptable and per-segment statistical validation is expensive.

Release carries the canary stage of that staged rollout onto live traffic [@martin_fowler_canary]. During the limited rollout, telemetry pipelines monitor inference latency, system stability, and prediction distributions. On the ranking service, a candidate receives 5 percent of live queries while the team compares click-through rate, p99 latency, and prediction drift against the baseline model. Only after the candidate demonstrates statistical stability without latency regressions is it promoted to serve full production traffic.

::: {#ws-ml-ops-knight-capital-error-2012 .callout-war-story title="The Knight Capital error (2012)"}

**Context**: Knight Capital Group was a major market maker in US equities handling over 17 percent of NYSE volume. In August 2012, an operational deployment updated SMARS, the firm's automated order-routing software, on seven of eight production servers but omitted the eighth [@sec2013knight].

**Mechanism**: The deployment repurposed a binary feature flag that, on the un-updated eighth server, activated Power Peg, an obsolete order-handling routine that had been left in the code. The stale server entered an un-throttled loop, transmitting parent order requests at $\sim 1{,}400\text{ orders/sec}$.

**Impact**: In 45 minutes, the router executed over 4 million unauthorized transactions covering more than 397 million shares, incurring a \$460 million loss. The firm survived only on emergency rescue financing raised days later, and lost its independence in an acquisition within months.

**Response**: The incident motivates verifying that every production node runs the intended version before it receives traffic, explicit feature-flag lifecycle controls, and circuit breakers that limit the damage a faulty release can cause.

**Systems lesson**: One server running the wrong version was enough to cause a \$460 million loss. ML deployments share this vulnerability: a model registry version mismatch, un-synchronized feature schemas, or partial canary routing can flood production with corrupted inference requests before telemetry alerts fire.

:::

Knight Capital shows why every node must be verified to run the intended version before traffic reaches it. Staged rollouts add a complementary protection by limiting how much traffic a bad version sees, but they can also expose load-dependent behavior. When canary deployments reveal anomalies at elevated traffic shares (such as memory exhaustion, queue spillover, or p99 tail latency inflation appearing at 30 percent traffic that remained undetectable at 5 percent), isolation requires systematic debugging across the stack. Effective diagnosis requires correlating multiple signals: performance benchmarking metrics, data distribution analysis to detect drift, and feature importance shifts that might explain degradation. Teams maintain debug toolkits including A/B test analysis frameworks, feature attribution tools, and data slice analyzers that identify which subpopulations are experiencing degraded performance.

That diagnosis loop must connect directly to the release pipeline. CI/CD integration automates deployment and rollback, but only when rollback is designed as part of the rollout mechanism rather than treated as an emergency script.

#### Rollback strategies and safety mechanisms {#sec-ml-operations-rollback-strategies-safety-mechanisms-7707}

Without reliable rollback\index{Rollback!strategies, safety mechanisms}[^fn-rollback-ml-deploy] capability, teams become deployment-averse and slow their iteration velocity. Effective rollback requires planning for three distinct scenarios:

[^fn-rollback-ml-deploy]: **Rollback (from database transaction management)**\index{Rollback!model state management}: This "undo" action for deployments is complicated in ML by model-dependent state (for example, cached embeddings), which may be incompatible between model versions. This mismatch can prolong recovery and contribute to deployment aversion and slower iteration.

The fastest tier, **immediate rollback**\index{Rollback!immediate}, addresses critical failures detected right after deployment: serving errors, latency spikes, or obvious prediction failures. It requires keeping the previous model version loaded and warm so traffic can switch without cold-start delay. **Rapid rollback**\index{Rollback!rapid} handles performance degradation detected through canary metrics soon after deployment, which requires model registry integration that keeps previous versions deployable with minimal configuration changes. **Delayed rollback**\index{Rollback!delayed} addresses subtle issues detected through business metrics or user feedback after full deployment, where rollback must account for model-dependent data such as personalization state or cached embeddings accumulated during the new model's operation.

@Tbl-rollback-patterns summarizes implementation patterns for each rollback type:

| **Rollback Type** | **Trigger**               | **Implementation**                   | **State Handling**              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------|:-------------------------------------|:--------------------------------|
| **Immediate**     | Serving errors, crashes   | Hot standby with fast routing switch | Verify state compatibility      |
| **Rapid**         | Canary metric degradation | Registry-based redeployment          | Clear caches, restart sessions  |
| **Delayed**       | Business metric decline   | Full redeployment with migration     | Migrate state, replay if needed |

: **Rollback Patterns by Scenario**: Each rollback type requires different infrastructure support and state handling strategies. Immediate rollback demands always-warm standbys; delayed rollback may require data migration procedures. {#tbl-rollback-patterns}

##### Rollback testing {.unnumbered}

Rollback procedures that have never been tested may fail when needed, and the gap is often discovered during an active incident, when cognitive load and time pressure are highest. Failure can stem from configuration dependencies, incompatible state, or unclear ownership. Periodic rollback exercises expose these gaps before they matter. Automated rollback criteria can shorten reaction time, but thresholds must be calibrated to the service and include safeguards against flapping. The restored model must also produce consistent behavior rather than predictions corrupted by stale caches or incompatible feature state. Step-by-step runbooks ensure that the responder need not be the person who designed the deployment.

##### Stateful vs. stateless rollback {.unnumbered}

ML systems vary in statefulness, which directly governs rollback complexity. For stateless workloads like tabular classification and static regression, rollback requires only swapping model weights or routing traffic back to the prior container, because individual inferences share no execution context. In contrast, stateful models (including sequential recommenders, session-based search rankers, and conversational systems) accumulate transient user state. Reverting such workloads can demand session resets, schema shims for cached context vectors, or explicit state migration; capturing versioned checkpoints at deployment boundaries mitigates this friction, but clean restoration remains an architectural property that requires empirical validation rather than assumption. The ranking service is the stateful case. It precalculates dense user and item embeddings and holds them in low-latency caches, so if version 2 rotates the latent vector space or changes the embedding dimension, the cached vectors become meaningless to a rolled-back version 1. A stateful rollback must therefore orchestrate atomic cache invalidation or dual-version namespace switching alongside weight redeployment to prevent scoring queries against incompatible vector spaces. The most complex failure mode arises in systems with feedback loops: when bad predictions pollute downstream feature logs or clickstream training sets during the degraded window, reverting the serving binary leaves contaminated data in the retraining corpus that must be expunged or quarantined before previous behavior is restored.

#### A/B testing for model validation {#sec-ml-operations-ab-testing-model-validation-e480}

A/B testing\index{A/B testing!statistical model validation} provides the statistical foundation for deployment decisions by comparing model versions under controlled conditions. Unlike canary deployments (which validate operational stability), A/B tests measure whether a new model improves business outcomes with statistical confidence.

##### Experiment setup and decision rules {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: ab-sample-size-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ A/B TEST SAMPLE SIZE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: A/B testing experimental design prose and @eq-ab-sample-size in
# │          @sec-ml-operations-ab-testing-model-validation-e480.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size a two-arm A/B deployment test for a conversion-rate lift.
# │ Show:    Roughly 745K users per variant detect a 2 percent relative lift.
# │ How:     Apply the standard two-proportion sample-size formula with
# │          NormalDist quantiles for confidence and power.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import ceil, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist
from mlsysim.physics import calc_two_proportion_sample_size
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check, fmt_percent, fmt_pp, fmt_rate, fmt_time

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class ABSampleSize:
    """Two-arm conversion-rate sample sizing for an A/B deployment test."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    confidence = 0.95
    power = 0.80
    baseline_rate = 0.05
    relative_lift = 0.02
    comparison_users_per_variant = 25_000

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha = 1 - confidence
    target_rate = baseline_rate * (1 + relative_lift)
    absolute_lift = target_rate - baseline_rate
    variance = baseline_rate * (1 - baseline_rate)
    z_alpha_2 = NormalDist().inv_cdf(1 - alpha / 2)
    z_beta = NormalDist().inv_cdf(power)
    users_per_variant = ceil(calc_two_proportion_sample_size(baseline_rate, absolute_lift, z_alpha=z_alpha_2, z_beta=z_beta))
    detectable_abs_lift = sqrt(2 * (z_alpha_2 + z_beta) ** 2 * variance / comparison_users_per_variant)
    detectable_pct_points = detectable_abs_lift * 100

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(740_000 <= users_per_variant <= 750_000, f"Expected about 745K users/variant, got {users_per_variant:,}.")
    check(0.5 <= detectable_pct_points <= 0.6, f"Expected about 0.5-0.6 percentage points, got {detectable_pct_points:.2f}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    confidence_pct_str = fmt_percent(confidence, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    power_pct_str = fmt_percent(power, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    baseline_pct_str = fmt_percent(baseline_rate, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    target_pct_str = fmt_percent(target_rate, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    relative_lift_pct_str = fmt_percent(relative_lift, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    users_per_variant_str = fmt(users_per_variant, precision=0, commas=True)
    comparison_users_per_variant_str = fmt(comparison_users_per_variant, precision=0, commas=True)
    detectable_pct_points_str = fmt_pp(detectable_pct_points, precision=1, commas=False, style="prose")
```

A valid A/B test establishes four controls to ensure deployment decisions remain statistically sound:

First, the **randomization unit**\index{A/B testing!randomization unit} specifies whether traffic is split by user ID or individual request. User-level hashing preserves consistency across sessions at the expense of larger sample requirements, whereas request-level splitting maximizes sample throughput but risks exposing a single user to alternating model variants.

Second, the statistical power envelope determines the traffic volume required to resolve meaningful differences. Under a common-variance Normal approximation, let $\RequiredUsersPerVariant$ be the required users per variant, $\MinimumDetectableEffect$ the minimum detectable effect, $\OutcomeStandardDeviation$ the outcome standard deviation (for a conversion metric, each user's outcome is a yes-or-no event, so $\OutcomeStandardDeviation^2$ is the baseline conversion rate times one minus that rate), and $\ConfidenceCriticalQuantile$ and $\PowerCriticalQuantile$ the positive standard-Normal critical values for the chosen two-sided confidence and power. The worked scenario uses `{python} ABSampleSize.confidence_pct_str` confidence and `{python} ABSampleSize.power_pct_str` power. @Eq-ab-sample-size translates those design targets into required traffic before launch.
$$\RequiredUsersPerVariant= \frac{2(\ConfidenceCriticalQuantile+ \PowerCriticalQuantile)^2 \OutcomeStandardDeviation^2}{\MinimumDetectableEffect^2}$$ {#eq-ab-sample-size}
For a `{python} ABSampleSize.relative_lift_pct_str` relative lift on a `{python} ABSampleSize.baseline_pct_str` baseline conversion rate (`{python} ABSampleSize.baseline_pct_str` to `{python} ABSampleSize.target_pct_str`) and `{python} ABSampleSize.power_pct_str` power, the experiment requires roughly `{python} ABSampleSize.users_per_variant_str` users per variant. If traffic limits the test to `{python} ABSampleSize.comparison_users_per_variant_str` users per variant instead, solving @eq-ab-sample-size for $\MinimumDetectableEffect$ shows that the test can detect only a much larger lift, about `{python} ABSampleSize.detectable_pct_points_str` absolute.

Third, **guardrail metrics**\index{Guardrail metric!A/B test constraint} define operational and behavioral boundaries that must not degrade even if the primary metric improves. A recommendation model improving click-through rate by 10 percent while increasing p99 response latency by 500 ms violates system guardrails and risks cascading timeouts across downstream services.

Fourth, a fixed evaluation horizon runs the test until the preregistered sample size and a minimum duration covering weekly seasonality are reached. Stopping the moment significance first appears inflates false positive rates through repeated peeking; sequential designs permit early stopping but need specialized analysis.

Those controls establish the statistical envelope, but ML systems add failure modes that ordinary web experiments can hide. Conversion events may arrive days after prediction, creating delayed feedback\index{A/B testing!delayed feedback, A/B testing challenges}: a recommendation shown Monday can drive a purchase Friday, so the attribution window must be part of the test design. Novelty effects\index{Novelty Effect!A/B testing bias} can also inflate early performance as users engage with fresh recommendations, which is why mature experiments include a burn-in period before measurement.

Ranking systems add interference effects, because showing an item to one user can change what remains available to another, which violates the independence assumption behind standard A/B analysis. Segment heterogeneity creates a second problem, since an overall neutral result may hide opposite effects in different cohorts. Guardrails, segment analysis, and preregistered decisions therefore belong to the experiment design.

@Tbl-ab-test-decisions turns those constraints into a deployment decision:

```{=latex}
\begingroup
%\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.3}
```

| **Primary Metric**          | **Guardrails** | **Decision**                                                                                                             |
|:----------------------------|:---------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Significant improvement** | All pass       | Ship new model                                                                                                           |
| **Significant improvement** | Some fail      | Investigate trade-offs, may need model iteration                                                                         |
| **No significant change**   | All pass       | Evidence inconclusive; retain current model unless a prespecified equivalence or noninferiority test supports the change |
| **Significant degradation** | N/A            | Do not ship; investigate root cause                                                                                      |

: **A/B Test Decision Matrix**: Deployment decisions should consider both primary metrics and guardrails. Improvements that come at the cost of guardrail violations require careful trade-off analysis rather than automatic deployment. {#tbl-ab-test-decisions tbl-colwidths="[25,15,60]"}

```{=latex}
\endgroup
```

The decision matrix is reliable only when the evaluation methodology is preregistered before launch. Teams must establish expected effect sizes, the randomization unit, attribution windows, guardrail thresholds, and minimum runtimes prior to observing production traffic.

Variance-reduction techniques such as CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data) [@deng2013improving] subtract the part of each user's outcome that pre-experiment behavior already predicts, shortening experiments without sacrificing power. Automated analysis pipelines protect the decision boundary from manual calculation errors, and archiving negative results discourages repeating unproductive architectures.

An A/B deployment decision is actionable only when the release machinery can promote, hold, or roll back the exact artifact that was evaluated, which is the guarantee the model registry of @sec-ml-operations-versioning-lineage-b1cf provides. The release path ends at the serving endpoint, whose internals belong to the serving system but whose stage timings operations relies on when a release misbehaves.

### Inference serving {#sec-ml-operations-inference-serving-3f9a}

Request scheduling, batching, and runtime selection belong to the serving system, and @sec-model-serving-latency-budget-ef40 shows that model inference is only one slice of end-to-end latency, and often not the largest (principle \ref{pri-latency-budget}). Operations uses that decomposition as a diagnostic instrument\index{Latency budget!end-to-end analysis}: when p99 regresses, per-stage timings for network, feature retrieval, parsing, inference, and serialization tell the on-call engineer which stage moved, and therefore which fix and which team the incident needs. Without stage-level tracing, every latency regression looks like a model problem, and the reflexive responses of rolling back or quantizing further cannot recover time lost in a feature store or a network hop (principle \ref{pri-amdahl}).

The endpoint contributes two of those stages, parsing and serialization, and its capacity model adds a third when it scales to zero. Protocol and serialization costs are developed in @sec-model-serving-interface-protocols-serialization-5510, and the cold start that scale-to-zero capacity pays after every idle period in @sec-model-serving-model-loading-initialization-cc5a. Operations inherits both as stages to trace, so that a regression in either is not mistaken for a model problem.


The keyword spotter keeps these operational goals (controlled rollout, fast rollback, stage-level telemetry) but changes the constraints under which they must be met, because its devices have limited power, memory, and connectivity.

### Edge AI deployment {#sec-ml-operations-edge-ai-deployment-patterns-dc1d}

Consider the keyword spotter after its detection drop. When its model degrades, an engineer cannot SSH into the device, roll back to a previous version, and restart. The device sits in someone's home on intermittent Wi-Fi, and its `{python} OpsRunningCases.kws_kb_str` model shares `{python} OpsRunningCases.flash_mib_str` of flash with the firmware that runs it. Every operational assumption from cloud MLOps (instant rollback, centralized logging, real-time monitoring) must be reimagined.

Edge AI\index{Edge AI!deployment patterns} runs machine learning inference at or near the data source rather than in centralized cloud infrastructure [@reddi2020]. Workloads governed by strict latency deadlines, bandwidth-constrained uplinks, data-privacy guarantees, or sub-watt power envelopes require executing inference directly on edge silicon. This operational paradigm introduces three interdependent systems constraints: resource limits, hierarchical tiered execution, and fail-safe over-the-air update mechanisms.

Resource constraints dominate edge deployment decisions. Edge devices require aggressive model optimization techniques (quantization, pruning, knowledge distillation) to meet the memory and power envelopes of microcontroller-class deployments [@warden2020tinyml; @david2021tensorflow]. Power budgets span four orders of magnitude, from milliwatts for IoT sensors to tens of watts in automotive systems, demanding power-aware inference scheduling and thermal management. Some hard real-time, safety-critical applications impose deterministic timing targets that require worst-case execution time\index{Worst-Case Execution Time!edge AI} (WCET) analysis under adverse conditions including thermal throttling and memory contention.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The quantization, pruning, and knowledge-distillation techniques that edge deployment relies on are established in @sec-model-compression.
:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol1_ml_ops_margin_003.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Vertical log-scale ladder of three orange bars, smallest at bottom: sensor at 1 mW, gateway at 1 W, automotive at tens of watts."}
:::

These constraints shape a natural deployment hierarchy across three tiers. Sensor-level processing handles immediate data filtering and feature extraction on microcontroller-class devices consuming 1–100&nbsp;mW. Edge gateway processing performs intermediate inference on application processors with 1–10&nbsp;W power budgets. Cloud coordination manages model distribution, aggregated learning, and complex reasoning requiring GPU-class resources. This hierarchy enables system-wide optimization, because computationally expensive operations migrate upward while latency-critical decisions remain local.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The memory and power envelopes that separate the edge, mobile, and TinyML tiers are established in @sec-ml-systems-tinyml-ubiquitous-sensing-scale-a67b.
:::

Two deployment contexts deserve specific attention. TinyML\index{TinyML!operational constraints} targets microcontroller-based inference under tight memory and milliwatt-class power constraints, requiring specialized engines such as TensorFlow Lite Micro and CMSIS-NN [@david2021tensorflow; @lai2018cmsis]. Model architectures must be co-designed with hardware constraints, favoring compact operators, quantization, and pruning strategies whose aggressiveness depends on the device and accuracy target. Mobile AI extends edge deployment to smartphones with moderate compute, using neural processing units (NPUs) and GPU compute shaders to meet interactive latency and battery-life constraints through power-aware scheduling.

Updates and monitoring complete the edge operational picture. Over-the-air (OTA) model updates\index{Over-the-air update!model distribution} enable maintenance for physically inaccessible systems. OTA pipelines need secure model distribution, artifact verification, and rollback mechanisms; delta or differential updates can reduce transfer volume when devices need not receive a complete model artifact. The keyword spotter's fail-safe OTA design uses dual-bank flash memory, a pattern common on microcontroller and embedded targets. The device keeps running from Bank A while it writes the candidate model and runtime to Bank B. After switching to Bank B, a hardware watchdog timer and a post-update self-test supervise the first inferences; if the new model triggers memory faults, hangs, or violates latency budgets, the bootloader automatically reverts execution to Bank A, preventing physically inaccessible devices from being bricked. Update scheduling must account for device connectivity patterns, power availability, and operational criticality.

Monitoring requires adaptation to resource-constrained environments: lightweight telemetry systems capture essential metrics (inference latency, power consumption, accuracy indicators) while minimizing overhead. Health monitoring tracks device-level conditions (thermal status, battery levels, connectivity quality) to predict maintenance needs. Edge-cloud coordination patterns enable adaptive offloading between tiers based on current load, network conditions, and latency requirements. Feature caching at edge gateways reduces redundant computation. Federated learning lets edge devices contribute model updates rather than raw training records, and secure aggregation and differential privacy limit what those updates reveal under an explicit threat model (@sec-responsible-engineering-technical-privacy-protection-methods-4a74 develops both).

Graceful degradation is a core operational pattern for edge AI. When thermal limits or battery depletion constrain hardware capacity, edge runtimes must dynamically shed load (downsampling input sample rates, bypassing speculative execution branches, or falling back to shallow heuristic models) within a fallback policy validated for the application's safety and quality requirements. Each of these controls, on the device and in the cloud, reserves resources for a version that serves little or no traffic, and the size of that reservation depends on the workload's regime.

### Memory and compute of release controls {#sec-ml-operations-release-control-footprint-c3e8}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: release-control-footprint-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEMORY AND COMPUTE HELD BY EACH RELEASE CONTROL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-ml-ops-release-control-footprint and the paragraph before it,
# │          closing @sec-ml-operations-production-operations-b76d.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that release safety for a capacity-bound model is paid in
# │          memory: every server-side control holds a second copy of the
# │          DLRM tables whatever share of traffic it serves.
# │ Show:    One copy needs two H100s, two copies need four; two FP16
# │          ResNet-50 copies are a fraction of one H100; the KWS dual-bank
# │          update holds a second 200 KB bank in 4 MiB of flash.
# │ How:     Registry model sizes over registry device capacities.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from math import ceil
from mlsysim import Models, Hardware, BYTES_INT8, BYTES_FP16
from mlsysim.core.units import GB, KB, MB, MiB
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class ReleaseControlFootprint:
    """Extra resident memory each release control holds on the DLRM service and the KWS device."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    dlrm = Models.Recommendation.DLRM
    h100 = Hardware.Cloud.H100
    resnet = Models.Vision.ResNet50
    kws = Models.Tiny.DS_CNN
    mcu = Hardware.Tiny.ESP32_S3
    canary_share = 0.05  # scenario: the 5 percent canary in the release-strategy prose

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    copy_bytes = dlrm.model_size
    accels_per_copy = ceil((copy_bytes / h100.memory.capacity).to("").magnitude)
    accels_two_copies = 2 * accels_per_copy
    resnet_bytes = resnet.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    resnet_two_copy_fraction = (2 * resnet_bytes / h100.memory.capacity).to("").magnitude
    kws_bank = kws.size_in_bytes(BYTES_INT8)
    flash = mcu.memory.flash_capacity

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(accels_per_copy == 2, f"Prose says one copy of the tables needs two H100s, got {accels_per_copy}.")
    check(accels_two_copies == 4, f"Prose says two copies need four H100s, got {accels_two_copies}.")
    check(resnet_two_copy_fraction < 0.01, "Two FP16 ResNet-50 copies should be a negligible fraction of one H100.")
    check(2 * kws_bank < flash, "Both KWS flash banks must fit the device's flash.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    copy_gb_str = fmt_memory(copy_bytes, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    accels_per_copy_str = fmt_int(accels_per_copy, commas=False)
    accels_two_copies_str = fmt_int(accels_two_copies, commas=False)
    canary_pct_str = fmt_percent(canary_share, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    canary_pct_sym_str = fmt_percent(canary_share, precision=0, commas=False, style='symbol')
    resnet_mb_str = fmt_memory(resnet_bytes, unit=MB, precision=1, commas=False)
    kws_bank_kb_str = fmt_memory(kws_bank, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    two_banks_kb_str = fmt_memory(2 * kws_bank, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    flash_mib_str = fmt_memory(flash, unit=MiB, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Every control in this section keeps a second version of the model alive, and for a capacity-bound model that second version, not the extra arithmetic, is the dominant cost (@tbl-ml-ops-release-control-footprint). A shadow deployment scores every request twice. A canary, an A/B test, and a blue-green switch divert traffic rather than adding work, yet each must hold the candidate's full embedding tables in accelerator memory whatever share of traffic it serves, and a hot standby for immediate rollback holds the previous version for the same reason. The ranking service's `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.canary_pct_str` canary therefore doubles the accelerators that hold tables, from two to four, while it carries a twentieth of the requests. A compute-bound ResNet-50 service pays the opposite way. Its `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.resnet_mb_str` of FP16 weights fit beside the serving copy on one accelerator, so its canary costs almost no memory and only its share of compute. The keyword spotter's dual-bank update costs flash instead of accelerator memory, a second `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.kws_bank_kb_str` bank that brings the model's share of the device's `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.flash_mib_str` to `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.two_banks_kb_str`.

| **Release control**                                                          | **Extra resident memory**                                                                                                                                                                  | **Extra inference work**                                                     | **What it buys**                                       |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| **Shadow deployment**                                                        | Second copy of the tables (`{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.copy_gb_str`); `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_per_copy_str` $\rightarrow$ `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_two_copies_str` H100s | Every request scored twice                                                   | Output and latency comparison with no user exposure    |
| **Canary (`{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.canary_pct_sym_str` of traffic)** | Second copy; `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_per_copy_str` $\rightarrow$ `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_two_copies_str` H100s                                            | None; a share of requests is diverted                                        | Live quality evidence on a bounded share of users      |
| **A/B test**                                                                 | Second copy; `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_per_copy_str` $\rightarrow$ `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_two_copies_str` H100s                                            | None; traffic is split between variants                                      | A statistically valid outcome comparison               |
| **Blue-green switch**                                                        | Full second environment; `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_per_copy_str` $\rightarrow$ `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_two_copies_str` H100s                                | Duplicate provisioned capacity during the switch                             | Rollback by a single routing change                    |
| **Hot standby**                                                              | Previous version resident; `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_per_copy_str` $\rightarrow$ `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.accels_two_copies_str` H100s                              | None until rollback                                                          | Immediate rollback without a cold start                |
| **KWS dual-bank update**                                                     | Second flash bank (`{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.kws_bank_kb_str` in `{python} ReleaseControlFootprint.flash_mib_str` of flash)                                                         | None                                                                         | Automatic revert after a failed update                 |

: **Release Controls on a Capacity-Bound Model**: Extra resident memory and inference work that each release control adds to the DLRM ranking service on H100 accelerators, and to the keyword spotter's flash. Every server-side control holds a second full copy of the embedding tables regardless of the traffic share it serves, so release safety for this model is paid in memory rather than arithmetic. {#tbl-ml-ops-release-control-footprint tbl-colwidths="[20,34,22,24]"}

::: {#chk-ml-ops-release-evidence .callout-checkpoint title="Evidence for a release"}

- [ ] **Promotion evidence**: A shadow model has acceptable latency and similar output distributions, but outcome labels have not arrived. What has been established, and what quality evidence is still missing?
- [ ] **Recovery state**: A canary changes an embedding dimension. Which artifacts and cached state must a tested rollback restore together?
- [ ] **Converted artifact**: Explain why passing aggregate accuracy before quantization does not replace numerical, slice-level, and runtime checks after conversion.

:::

Getting a model into production, and back out again, is only half the operational challenge. A successfully released model can still degrade through distribution shift or corrupted upstream features without raising runtime errors, and none of the controls above will notice. Production monitoring supplies the evidence that tells the team a release, a rollback, or a retraining run is needed at all.

## Production Monitoring {#sec-ml-operations-production-monitoring-5e1b}

*A deployed model loses accuracy at a rate that must be measured rather than assumed.* Every decision left in the operations loop (retrain, roll back, or wait) rests on evidence that only production monitoring can supply, including the decay rate that the retraining economics of @sec-ml-operations-retraining-decisions-7d3a must fit. An ML service is correct only while its live inputs resemble the data it learned from, so as they change (the system entropy of @sec-ml-systems-system-entropy-9c4e), predictive quality may decline. Monitoring is where the third critical interface, production-monitoring, makes that risk observable. Staged rollout paired with input and outcome monitoring lets teams investigate failing versions and limit their impact, within the time needed to collect evidence.

### Infrastructure telemetry and hardware utilization {#sec-ml-operations-quantifying-drift-physics-psi-8c11}

Confirming whether predictive quality has changed, and by how much, requires ground-truth labels that often arrive with substantial delay, so monitoring cannot wait for outcomes alone. In production, serving failures span two fundamentally different physical regimes: immediate hardware execution bottlenecks and gradual distributional drift. Disentangling them requires two distinct telemetry layers: infrastructure metrics that reveal whether the serving system itself is compute-, memory-, or I/O-bound, and distribution and outcome metrics that connect data movement to model performance.

The first layer is infrastructure-level monitoring, which tracks indicators such as CPU and GPU utilization, memory bandwidth, disk consumption, network latency, and service availability. Measuring GPU utilization alone is incomplete; an accelerator reporting high execution time may still be stalled waiting for DRAM or PCIe transfers, while low utilization often signals host-side preprocessing bottlenecks. Correlating kernel execution times with memory bandwidth utilization and input pipeline queue depths distinguishes compute-, memory-, and I/O-bound behavior.

Power-efficiency metrics (such as inferences per joule or FLOP/s/W, depending on workload) add a cost-normalized view that enables mixed-workload scheduling. Thermal monitoring similarly informs operational scheduling, particularly under sustained high load where thermal throttling forces hardware clocks down, introducing tail-latency spikes that violate SLOs. An MLOps telemetry pipeline incorporates thermal headroom metrics to steer traffic across available accelerators before throttling occurs. Time-series engines such as Prometheus[^fn-prometheus-mlops-monitoring] [@prometheus], Grafana [@grafana], and Elastic [@elastic] collect and visualize these operational metrics across the serving fleet.

[^fn-prometheus-mlops-monitoring]: **Prometheus**\index{Prometheus!monitoring trade-off}: Prometheus periodically scrapes targets and stores time series for aggregation. Scrape and rule-evaluation intervals jointly affect alert latency and may miss short excursions. Monitoring per-accelerator thermals allows precise workload routing at higher data cost, while server-level aggregates can mask component-level throttling.

Alerts convert these signals into intervention before silent degradation reaches downstream consumers. A sustained drop in model accuracy triggers drift investigation; infrastructure alerts signal memory saturation, thermal throttling, or degraded network throughput. The latency of these alerts governs the window of undetected failure. Alerts must record the model version, affected input subpopulation, and triggering aggregation window so responders can isolate and reproduce the failure state.

::: {#exmp-ml-ops-recommender-monitoring-at-scale .callout-example title="Recommendation monitoring at scale"}

**Scenario**: Consider the ranking service at high throughput, its latency within the SLO while recommendation quality declined as user behavior changed.

**Diagnosis**: Traditional infrastructure metrics (CPU utilization, HTTP error rates) remained green while cohort-level CTR fell. The engagement decline motivates investigation of traffic, feature pipelines, and ranking behavior; it does not establish classification accuracy loss.

**Systems lesson**: Infrastructure telemetry alone cannot establish recommendation quality. Cohort-level outcome tracking exposes localized engagement changes, while matched comparisons and mature labels are needed to assess predictive-quality changes and their causes.

:::

#### Hardware utilization patterns {#sec-ml-operations-hardware-utilization-patterns-5c10}

Standard administrative GPU utilization metrics\index{GPU!utilization monitoring}, such as the reading from `nvidia-smi`, report the fraction of time a kernel is executing rather than the fraction of peak arithmetic throughput achieved, the distinction between busy time and model FLOPs utilization (MFU) drawn in @sec-model-training-identifying-bottlenecks-f57f. The ranking service's gathers of non-contiguous embedding vectors can therefore hold a high utilization reading while every resident warp stalls on memory, and a green gauge on the operations dashboard says nothing about compute efficiency.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The analytical model separating compute-bound execution from memory-bandwidth saturation across arithmetic intensities is established in @sec-hardware-acceleration-roofline-model-42ff.
:::

Distinguishing compute execution from memory or pipeline stalls requires evaluating streaming multiprocessor (SM) execution efficiency alongside memory bandwidth and I/O saturation. @Tbl-gpu-utilization-patterns gives illustrative screening patterns. Here GPU utilization is kernel-active time; measured FLOP rate, execution traces, and relevant stall counters are needed to test the proposed bottleneck:

| **Pattern**                  |   **GPU Util**   | **Memory bandwidth util.** | **Optimization Strategy**                                             |
|:-----------------------------|:----------------:|:--------------------------:|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Possible compute limit**   |       >85%       |            <70%            | Check achieved FLOP rate; evaluate faster kernels or compute capacity |
| **Possible bandwidth limit** |      50–85%      |            >85%            | Check traffic and stalls; evaluate quantization or memory access      |
| **Possible input limit**     |       <50%       |            <50%            | Trace input starvation before changing prefetch or storage            |
| **Batch-starved**            | Variable (spiky) |          Variable          | Dynamic batching, request queuing on single server                    |

: **GPU Utilization Patterns**: Illustrative utilization signatures suggest hypotheses, not unique diagnoses. High kernel-active time does not establish compute saturation. Confirm candidates with achieved arithmetic throughput, memory traffic, stall counters, and an execution trace before choosing an optimization. {#tbl-gpu-utilization-patterns tbl-colwidths="[15,15,23,47]"}

Each candidate maps to a term of the iron law of ML systems\index{Iron law of ML systems!production monitoring} (principle \ref{pri-iron-law}): the compute-bound signature to $\Operations/(\PeakRate \cdot \EfficiencyHw)$, the memory-bound signature to $\DataVolume/\Bandwidth$, and low utilization of both to the data pipeline, so the trace and counters guide which term to investigate when a latency SLO is violated.

Utilization targets differ by workload. Batch training and batch (static) inference\index{Batch inference!utilization targets}, which tolerates queuing and offline scheduling, can run above 80 to 85 percent kernel-active time while the team measures useful throughput. **Online inference**\index{Online inference!definition} instead targets 50--70 percent of measured sustainable capacity at median load, holding back headroom so that bursts do not cascade into p99 timeouts (@sec-model-serving-queuing-theory-tail-latency-29a6). These figures are diagnostic starting points rather than thresholds, because kernel-active time and demand relative to capacity have different denominators.

For large language model (LLM)\index{LLM!KV-cache serving} serving, KV-cache\index{KV cache!LLM serving bottleneck} utilization on each node, the per-request store of past attention state, is a capacity-planning signal, because near the limit the scheduler must queue or reject requests, shrink batches, or shorten the admissible context (@sec-model-serving-memory-kv-cache-d1ea sizes and schedules the cache).

Utilization and memory telemetry also feed the number the business sees. Cost per inference\index{Cost per inference!operational tracking}, the hourly accelerator bill divided by sustained throughput, is defined and worked out in @sec-model-serving-cost-per-inference-27fc; operationally it belongs on the same dashboard as the utilization signatures in @tbl-gpu-utilization-patterns, because a rising cost per thousand inferences at constant pricing is often the first visible symptom of efficiency erosion (smaller effective batches, a shift in traffic mix, or a regression that stays inside the latency SLO).

### Statistical monitoring and drift detection {#sec-ml-operations-model-infrastructure-monitoring-3988}

Infrastructure telemetry shows how the serving hardware behaves; statistical monitoring\index{Model monitoring!performance tracking}\index{Model monitoring!drift detection} shows whether the model's predictions remain correct. Unit tests can verify deterministic components but cannot by themselves establish population-level predictive performance, which must be estimated statistically. Monitoring implements observable degradation (@sec-ml-operations-mlops-3ea3), transforming this theoretical limitation into operational practice. Once monitoring surfaces a symptom (a latency SLO miss, throughput below target, or memory creep), @sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy-bottleneck-diagnostic-3fc9 maps that symptom to its dominant D·A·M term and tells the operator which optimizations will move the binding constraint and which will be wasted on serving infrastructure. Without continuous monitoring and the deeper **observability**\index{Observability!system state inference} it enables (the ability to infer internal state from outputs), teams lack the evidence needed to distinguish a healthy model from an unobserved regression.

Effective monitoring spans both infrastructure health and statistical model behavior. On the infrastructure side, metrics track hardware saturation, memory allocation, and latency distributions. On the model side, teams track evaluation metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and confusion matrix shifts [@scikit_learn_confusion_matrix] across live prediction streams.

Those quality metrics require joining predictions to outcomes under a fixed evaluation horizon. Consider a conversion model whose prediction log records a request identifier, prediction time, score, and the immutable version actually served. The outcome log records the same identifier, event time, and observation time. For an older request served by the previous version, a purchase event within the horizon supplies a positive label once observed; a completed observation window with no purchase supplies a negative label, provided outcome collection is complete. A recent request served by the candidate with no recorded purchase remains pending until its horizon and the permitted reporting delay have elapsed. The absence of a purchase record while that window is open is unknown, not a negative outcome. Joining by identifier and retaining the served version attributes each completed outcome to the model that made the prediction rather than to whichever model is deployed when the label arrives.

A quality comparison groups predictions by serving period and version, then evaluates cohorts whose outcome windows have matured under the same horizon and reporting policy, with comparable traffic conditions. Each metric and slice must report label coverage, the fraction of eligible predictions with resolved outcomes. An apparent drop caused by comparing the candidate's pending outcomes with the previous version's completed outcomes does not justify retraining; it calls for completing the window or repairing outcome collection. Even a mature window can contain selective labels if outcomes are observed only for exposed recommendations or reviewed transactions. Coverage and collection-policy checks must accompany uncertainty estimates before a quality regression supports diagnosis and a retraining decision.

Statistical monitoring has to separate two axes of distribution shift,[^fn-drift-types-ops] because they differ in what a monitor can observe. Write the input distribution as $\InputDistribution$ and the relationship between inputs and labels as $\ConditionalDistribution$. The degradation equation compares $\TrainingDistribution$ and $\CurrentDistribution$, the training-time and serving-time measurements of that same data distribution. Data drift is a change in $\InputDistribution$, of which covariate shift[^fn-drift-covariate-shift] is the special case in which $\ConditionalDistribution$ stays stable, and concept drift\index{Concept drift!changing relationships} is a change in $\ConditionalDistribution$ itself. The drift taxonomy is defined in @sec-data-engineering-detecting-responding-data-drift-509a, where the keyword spotter's microphone change is the worked case.

[^fn-drift-types-ops]: **Label-free vs. label-dependent detection**\index{Drift detection delay!label latency}: A change in $\InputDistribution$ can be estimated from sufficient input samples without labels, although detection is not immediate. A change in $\ConditionalDistribution$ generally requires labeled outcomes, which in high-stakes domains (medical diagnosis, fraud detection, legal decisions) can take days, weeks, or months. Proxy metrics such as prediction-confidence distributions and output entropy can provide imperfect early warnings that trade false-alarm rate for detection speed.

[^fn-drift-covariate-shift]: **Covariate shift**\index{Drift!covariate shift}: Importance-weighting corrections for covariate shift assume that the support of the training distribution covers the deployment distribution: every deployment input could have appeared in training, just with different probability. When deployment contains genuinely out-of-distribution inputs (new product categories, new demographics, adversarial inputs), the correction can fail and the model can produce confidently wrong outputs with no warning signal, making support coverage the hidden assumption that determines whether drift correction or full retraining may be required.

Operations adds one distinction that the definitions alone do not make. **Model decay**\index{Model decay!definition} is the observed decline in prediction quality over time while the model code stays unchanged, and data drift is only one possible cause of it, alongside concept drift and changes in the surrounding pipeline. Monitoring model outputs alone can miss input drift or mistake a benign output change for quality loss, so operations also tracks the input feature statistics behind the divergence $\StatisticalDivergence$, measured with PSI\index{Population stability index!drift detection}, KS tests\index{Kolmogorov-Smirnov test!continuous drift}, or the Wasserstein distance, also called earth mover's distance\index{Earth mover's distance!multi-dimensional drift} (the probability mass that must move, and how far, to turn one distribution into the other). These statistics can warn earlier than labeled performance because ground-truth feedback is often delayed.

The signature of data drift in live telemetry is a feature distribution that moves in step with a quality metric, and three synchronized telemetry tiers aligned over time expose how covariate shift erodes model performance (@fig-data-drift). Across the top panel, discrete request samples transition from predominantly green (online sales) to orange (in-store sales); the figure's "online store" and "offline store" labels name sales channels, not the feature-store tiers of @sec-ml-operations-feature-stores-c01c. The middle panel charts this shift as an expanding offline area in the sales_channel feature distribution, directly matching the steep decline of the model accuracy curve in the bottom panel. This temporal alignment motivates comparing input feature distributions with outcome metrics; their co-movement supplies a diagnostic hypothesis rather than establishing the cause by itself.

::: {#fig-data-drift fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Data Drift Impact**: In this illustrative scenario, incoming samples shift from predominantly online to increasingly offline sales while model accuracy declines over the same interval. Monitoring inputs and outcomes together helps determine whether the distribution shift is associated with the loss in accuracy." fig-alt="Three horizontally aligned panels over time. The top panel shows incoming samples as green and orange blocks. The middle panel shows the sales_channel feature distribution changing from a green Online store region to an expanding orange Offline store region. The bottom panel shows a green model-accuracy curve declining from left to right."}

```{.tikz}
\begin{tikzpicture}[line join=round,font=\sffamily,outer sep=0pt]
\tikzset{
```
